claims.text: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi can be prepared as a single-phase solid solution with minimal grain-boundary and precipitation effects.
Substituting 5–10 at% of a constituent with a substantially different-sized solute increases atomic size mismatch.
Greater solute atomic size mismatch increases local lattice distortion.
Increased local lattice distortion strengthens interactions between dislocations and the surrounding lattice.
Stronger dislocation–lattice interactions pin dislocations and raise the energy barrier for dislocation motion.
Dislocation pinning caused by lattice distortion increases yield strength.
Dislocation pinning caused by lattice distortion increases hardness.
At approximately 300 K and modest strain rates, thermally activated deformation and phase-transformation effects are minimal.
Under the stated temperature and strain-rate conditions, lattice distortion is the dominant strengthening mechanism.
Variants having greater lattice distortion will exhibit statistically significant increases in yield strength relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Variants having greater lattice distortion will exhibit statistically significant increases in hardness relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The proposed behavior is limited to microstructures that remain single-phase solid solutions without precipitation.
Outside the single-phase, ambient-temperature, modest-strain-rate regime, other strengthening mechanisms may dominate.
The quantitative hardness and strength changes depend on the magnitude of the solute atomic size mismatch.
Precipitation and grain-boundary strengthening could obscure the proposed lattice-distortion effect.
Failure to observe statistically significant increases in both hardness and yield strength in higher-mismatch, single-phase variants would falsify the hypothesis.
Observation of precipitation or another phase change in a variant would falsify the single-phase lattice-distortion hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary restricts the hypothesis to single-phase, precipitation-free alloys, but the falsification rule treats precipitation or a phase change as falsification. Such a sample falls outside the stated domain and would normally invalidate the controlled comparison rather than falsify the within-domain mechanism.
